back2basics.text: GST is an indirect tax levied on the supply of goods and services across India, replacing multiple indirect taxes to create a unified tax structure. It is collected at each stage of the supply chain, with input tax credits available to avoid cascading taxes. GST revenues are shared between the Centre and States, and the GST Council governs rates and rules to ensure uniformity and compliance.

2026-11-01-pm-530889d215.deck: Gross GST collections in October 2026 surged 23% year-on-year to ₹2.31 lakh crore, driven by festive demand and strong domestic and import revenues. This data reflects the resilience of the Indian economy and improved tax compliance, important for understanding fiscal policy and indirect taxation.

back2basics.concept: Energy security and coal import dependence
back2basics.text: Energy security means ensuring reliable and affordable energy supply to meet a country's needs. Coal is a major energy source for power generation and industry in India. Import dependence on coal can expose the economy to international market fluctuations and supply disruptions. Increasing domestic coal production and improving supply chains help reduce this dependence, enhancing energy security and economic stability.

2026-11-01-pm-6f6fe28ad1.deck: India's total coal imports fell by 5.83% in August 2026 compared to the previous year, reflecting efforts to reduce import dependence by boosting domestic coal production. This development is important for UPSC aspirants as it relates to energy security, economic policy, and environmental concerns.

structure.intro: Introduce the context of India's coal import decline in August 2026.

mcq.stem:
Consider the following statements about India's coal imports in August 2026:
1. Total coal imports declined by 5.83% compared to August 2025.
2. Coal imports by imported coal-based power plants decreased by 0.98% in the same period.
mcq.trap: Statement 2 is incorrect because imports by imported coal-based power plants marginally increased by 0.98%, not decreased.

body.label: Overall decline
body.text: India's total coal imports decreased by 5.83%, falling from 111.05 million tonnes in August 2025 to 104.57 million tonnes in August 2026.

body.label: Power sector imports
body.text: Coal imports by power plants declined by 6.39%, from 22.77 million tonnes to 21.32 million tonnes, reflecting improved domestic coal availability.

body.label: Imported coal-based plants
body.text: Imports by imported coal-based power plants marginally increased by 0.98%, from 18.13 million tonnes to 18.31 million tonnes, as these plants primarily use imported coal.

body.label: Blending coal imports
body.text: Coal imports for blending at domestic coal-based power plants dropped sharply by 35.23%, from 4.64 million tonnes to 3.00 million tonnes, indicating reduced blending needs.

body.label: Coking coal imports
body.text: Coking coal imports, vital for the steel industry, declined by 4.18%, from 28.49 million tonnes to 27.30 million tonnes due to domestic supply constraints.

body.label: Import share in consumption
body.text: The share of imported coal in total coal consumption decreased from 21.20% to 19.30%, showing reduced reliance on imports.

sections.heading: What are the key trends in India's coal imports in August 2026?

body.label: Energy security
body.text: Reducing coal import dependence strengthens India's energy security by relying more on domestic coal production.

body.label: Economic benefits
body.text: Lower imports reduce foreign exchange outflow and improve the trade balance, supporting economic stability.

body.label: Environmental impact
body.text: Improved domestic coal supply and reduced imports can help manage coal quality and emissions, contributing to environmental goals.

body.label: Industrial supply
body.text: Stable coal supply supports uninterrupted power generation and steel production, critical for industrial growth.

sections.heading: Why does the decline in coal imports matter for India?

body.label: Boosting domestic production
body.text: The Ministry of Coal focuses on increasing domestic coal production and offtake to meet demand.

body.label: Improving infrastructure
body.text: Efforts include strengthening First Mile Connectivity and coal evacuation infrastructure to ensure timely coal supply.

body.label: Coordination with agencies
body.text: The Ministry coordinates with the Ministry of Railways, Coal India Limited, and subsidiaries to maintain coal stocks and supply.

body.label: Supply chain efficiency
body.text: Measures to improve supply-chain efficiency aim to reduce avoidable import dependence and support power and industrial sectors.

back2basics.text: Poverty is often measured by income thresholds such as the extreme poverty line, which is the minimum income needed to meet basic needs. The World Bank uses international poverty lines like $3 per day at purchasing power parity to compare poverty across countries. Inequality is measured by indices like the Gini Index, where a lower value indicates more equal income distribution. Understanding these measures helps evaluate socio-economic progress.

2026-11-01-pm-d416913932.deck: Prime Minister Modi highlighted a World Bank report showing a sharp fall in India's extreme poverty from 27.1% in 2011 to 2.6% in 2023, reflecting a major socio-economic shift. This matters for UPSC aspirants as it relates to poverty alleviation, economic inequality, and employment growth, key topics in GS3 Economy and GS1 Social Issues.

structure.intro: India has witnessed a historic decline in extreme poverty between 2011 and 2023, as highlighted by the World Bank.

mcq.stem:
Consider the following statements about India's poverty decline as per the World Bank report cited by PM Modi:
1. India's extreme poverty rate dropped from 27.1% in 2011 to 2.6% in 2023.
2. Employment grew by 13.4 crore in six years, which is less than the increase in the working-age population.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
mcq.trap: Statement 2 is incorrect because employment growth of 13.4 crore in six years was nearly twice the increase in the working-age population, not less.

body.label: Extreme poverty rate drop
body.text: India's extreme poverty rate fell from 27.1% in 2011 to 2.6% in 2023, based on the $3 per day poverty line at 2021 PPP.

body.label: People lifted out of poverty
body.text: Between 2011 and 2023, 49.6 crore people moved out of extreme poverty in India.

body.label: Measurement thresholds
body.text: The report uses the lower-middle-income poverty threshold of $4.20 per day and the extreme poverty line of $3 per day at 2021 PPP to estimate poverty.

sections.heading: What does the World Bank report say about India's poverty decline?

body.label: Employment growth
body.text: Employment increased by 13.4 crore in six years, nearly twice the growth of the working-age population, indicating improved job opportunities.

body.label: Reduction in inequality
body.text: India's Gini Index, a measure of economic inequality, fell by over 20% to 23.0, showing a significant decrease in income disparity.

body.label: Multidimensional poverty reduction
body.text: The report highlights progress not only in monetary poverty but also in non-monetary indicators, reflecting broader socio-economic development.

sections.heading: Why does this poverty decline matter for India’s economy and society?

body.label: Public messaging

Disaster management involves preparedness, early warning systems, relief, and rehabilitation efforts to reduce the impact of such natural calamities on vulnerable communities like fisherfolk.

body.label: Cyclone formation
body.text: Cyclone Murasu has formed over the Bay of Bengal, prompting weather warnings and high alert status in Andhra Pradesh and Odisha.

body.label: Impact on fishing
body.text: Frequent weather warnings and fishing bans have paralyzed maritime trade and disrupted supply chains, severely affecting the coastal fishing community.

sections.heading: What is the current situation with Cyclone Murasu?

body.label: Financial crisis
body.text: Repeated fishing bans since June have caused cumulative losses exceeding ₹36 crore for coastal Andhra Pradesh's fisherfolk.

body.label: Livelihood disruption
body.text: Cyclone Arnab, a previous storm, caused a direct trade loss of nearly ₹20 crore due to a six-day fishing ban, with over 60% of the fishing fleet remaining anchored during adverse weather.

body.label: Wider economic effects
body.text: Low prices for commercial fish varieties have further hurt vendors, auctioneers, ice suppliers, and transport operators, compounding the economic distress.

sections.heading: Why does Cyclone Murasu matter for coastal fisherfolk?

body.label: Demand for compensation
body.text: Fisherfolk organisations have petitioned for 100% financial compensation for damaged gear and craft affecting 3.32 lakh active marine fishermen statewide.

body.label: Subsistence allowance
body.text: They also demand a daily subsistence allowance of ₹600 per fisherman for seven days of forced idleness due to fishing bans.

body.label: Relief fund provisions
body.text: The petitioners argue compensation should be aligned with the expanded Chief Minister’s Relief Fund provisions under G.O. Ms. No. 1 (2025) rather than the more restrictive State Disaster Response Fund limits.
